This tutorial assesses extreme heat risk in [Pergamino](https://www.pergamino.gob.ar), a partido in the north of Buenos Aires Province, Argentina.
It combines the hazard, exposure, and vulnerability framework with open data that you can query in place.
Every layer except one comes from a cloud-optimized file on [Source Cooperative](https://source.coop/) or an open S3 bucket, and the code reads only the part that covers Pergamino.

The [source of this page](https://github.com/nlebovits/landsat-lst-pipeline/blob/main/docs/tutorials/pergamino.qmd) is a Quarto document.
To run it yourself, install the documentation dependencies and start a live preview from the repository root:

```bash
uv sync --group docs
uv run --group docs quarto preview docs/tutorials/pergamino.qmd
```

If you have not used the surface temperature product before, start with the [quickstart](/quickstart.qmd).
The [known issues](/about/known-issues.qmd) page lists the limits of the data that this analysis inherits.

## Introduction

This tutorial answers four questions for Pergamino, and its code adapts to another city:

- How many days above 35 °C does the climate record show, and how many do the models project?
- Which parts of the city run hottest on hot days?
- How much do tree canopy and buildings explain the pattern?
- Who lives in the hottest places, and how many of them are vulnerable?

The analysis ends with five recommendations that apply under every emissions scenario.
The [sensable-heat web map](https://sensable-heat.vercel.app/) displays the same data, and you can browse its layers for any city.
For the reasoning behind the product, listen to the [Great Data Products episode with Elizabeth Wesley](https://greatdataproducts.com/episodes/2026/09/wesley-heat-data/).

### Set up

The first cell loads the libraries and a small plotting module, [`docs/_plotting.py`](https://github.com/nlebovits/landsat-lst-pipeline/blob/main/docs/_plotting.py).
That module defines the figure style, the colormaps, and the dimmed imagery basemap that every map on this site shares.

```{python}
#| label: setup
import io
import math
import sys
import time
import warnings
from pathlib import Path

import duckdb
import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pystac
import rasterio
import shapely
from affine import Affine
from IPython.display import Markdown
from matplotlib import patheffects
from matplotlib.colors import BoundaryNorm, LinearSegmentedColormap, LogNorm
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from rasterio.enums import Resampling
from rasterio.features import rasterize, shapes
from rasterio.warp import reproject, transform_bounds
from rasterio.windows import Window, from_bounds
from shapely.geometry import box

# Quarto runs this notebook from its own folder or from the project root.
# Look in both places for the docs folder, which holds _plotting.py.
DOCS_DIR = next(
    p
    for p in [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents, Path.cwd() / "docs"]
    if (p / "_plotting.py").exists()
)
sys.path.insert(0, str(DOCS_DIR))
import _plotting as plot  # noqa: E402

plot.apply_style()
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="Mean of empty slice")
T0 = time.perf_counter()


def n(x):
    """A count with thousands separators."""
    return f"{x:,.0f}"


def md_table(df, floatfmt="{:,.1f}"):
    """Render a DataFrame as a Markdown table, which Quarto styles natively."""
    def cell(v):
        if isinstance(v, float):
            return floatfmt.format(v)
        if isinstance(v, (int, np.integer)):
            return f"{v:,}"
        return str(v)

    head = "| " + " | ".join(df.columns) + " |"
    rule = "|" + "|".join("---" for _ in df.columns) + "|"
    rows = ["| " + " | ".join(cell(v) for v in row) + " |" for row in df.itertuples(index=False)]
    return Markdown("\n".join([head, rule, *rows]))
```

## Study area

Pergamino's municipal spatial data infrastructure publishes the boundaries this analysis needs, from the partido down to each barrio.
The [IDE Pergamino mirror](https://source.coop/nlebovits/pergamino-ide) on Source Cooperative republishes every collection as GeoParquet.
[DuckDB](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/extensions/spatial/overview) reads each file over HTTP without downloading it.

The urban agglomerations carry the municipality's own classification, which this analysis keeps:

- **Urban** (`urbana`): the continuous built-up city.
- **Peri-urban** (`periurbana`): the mixed fringe of the city, where houses, industry, and fields meet.
- **Rural settlement** (`urbano en ruralidad`): the small towns scattered across the agricultural partido.

```{python}
#| label: study-area
con = duckdb.connect()
con.sql("INSTALL spatial; LOAD spatial; INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;")
con.sql("SET s3_region = 'us-west-2'; SET enable_progress_bar = false;")


def read_geoparquet(sql):
    """Run a DuckDB query that returns WKB in `geometry`; return a GeoDataFrame."""
    df = con.sql(sql).df()
    geometry = gpd.GeoSeries.from_wkb(df.pop("geometry").apply(bytes), crs="EPSG:4326")
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(df, geometry=geometry)


partido = read_geoparquet(f"""
    SELECT departa AS name, ST_AsWKB(geometry) AS geometry
    FROM '{IDE_URL}/limites/partido_pergamino/publico_partido_pergamino.parquet'
""")
aglomerados = read_geoparquet(f"""
    SELECT id, clasificacion, distrito, ST_AsWKB(geometry) AS geometry
    FROM '{IDE_URL}/limites/aglomerados_urbanos/publico_aglomerados_urbanos.parquet'
""")
barrios = read_geoparquet(f"""
    SELECT id, nombre, ST_AsWKB(geometry) AS geometry
    FROM '{IDE_URL}/limites/barrios/publico_barrios.parquet'
""")

URBAN_CLASSES = list(plot.URBAN_CLASS_COLORS)
class_area_km2 = (
    aglomerados.to_crs(AREA_CRS)
    .assign(area=lambda d: d.area / 1e6)
    .groupby("clasificacion")["area"]
    .sum()
    .reindex(URBAN_CLASSES)
)
partido_area_km2 = float(partido.to_crs(AREA_CRS).area.sum() / 1e6)
urban_share = 100 * class_area_km2.sum() / partido_area_km2
n_towns = aglomerados.query("clasificacion == 'urbano en ruralidad'").distrito.nunique()

city = aglomerados[aglomerados.clasificacion != "urbano en ruralidad"]
city_frame = city.total_bounds
city_outline = gpd.GeoSeries([city.union_all()], crs="EPSG:4326").boundary
```

The partido covers `{python} n(partido_area_km2)` km², and the three urban classes cover `{python} f"{class_area_km2.sum():.0f}"` km² of it, or `{python} f"{urban_share:.1f}"`%.
The city of Pergamino holds `{python} f"{class_area_km2['urbana']:.0f}"` km² of urban land, and `{python} n_towns` rural settlements add `{python} f"{class_area_km2['urbano en ruralidad']:.0f}"` km² more.
The city's `{python} len(barrios)` barrios become the units of the summary in [Risk by barrio](#risk-by-barrio).

#| fig-alt: "Two maps. The left map shows the large rural partido of Pergamino with a dark outline, a compact blue city near its center ringed by orange peri-urban patches, and small green rural towns scattered across the fields. The right map zooms into the city, showing blue urban land divided by thin black barrio boundaries and orange peri-urban land on its fringes."

ax_p.annotate("City of Pergamino", xy=(x1, y1), xytext=(6, 6), textcoords="offset points",

## Climate projections: how hot will it get?

Start with the climate record, because a local map makes sense only against a trend.
A mayor already knows that summers are hot.
A baseline count of extreme heat days, and the count the models project for the coming decades, turns that knowledge into a trajectory that a budget can plan against.
The local analysis that follows then shows where in the city to act.

The indicator is the number of days per year with a maximum temperature above 35 °C.
The World Resources Institute's [Cool Cities Lab](https://coolcities.wri.org/) uses this threshold, above which sustained heat stress becomes dangerous.
A count of days also maps onto an emergency protocol: you can set one to activate on such a day.

::: {.callout-note}
## Shared socioeconomic pathways

Each Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) describes one possible future of emissions and development:

- **SSP1-2.6, low emissions:** steep cuts in emissions, about 1.8 °C of warming by 2100.
- **SSP2-4.5, intermediate emissions:** moderate mitigation, about 2.7 °C of warming by 2100.
- **SSP5-8.5, high emissions:** continued dependence on fossil fuels, about 4.4 °C of warming by 2100.

Nobody knows which path the world takes.
A plan that holds under all three is more useful than a plan tuned to one.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## The one dataset in this repository

The [IPCC WGI Interactive Atlas](https://interactive-atlas.ipcc.ch/) publishes `tx35` as global NetCDF files behind the Copernicus [Climate Data Store](https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/datasets/projections-climate-atlas).
Reading them requires a CDS account, an API key, and several hundred megabytes of downloads.
Instead, the repository includes a small extract for Pergamino's grid cell, [`pergamino_tx35.parquet`](https://github.com/nlebovits/landsat-lst-pipeline/blob/main/docs/tutorials/data/pergamino_tx35.parquet), along with the [script that made it](https://github.com/nlebovits/landsat-lst-pipeline/blob/main/docs/tutorials/data/extract_tx35.py).
The same folder stores the CDS [provenance records](https://github.com/nlebovits/landsat-lst-pipeline/tree/main/docs/tutorials/data/provenance) for the four downloads.
To extract another city, download the four experiments with the CDS API and run the script with that city's coordinates.
:::

```{python}
#| label: climate
tx35 = pd.read_parquet(TX35_PATH)
cell_lon, cell_lat = float(tx35.lon.iloc[0]), float(tx35.lat.iloc[0])

# Annual totals per model run. A year with a missing month is left out.
annual = (
    tx35.groupby(["experiment", "member", "year"])["tx35"]
    .agg(["sum", "count"])
    .query("count == 12")["sum"]
    .rename("days")
    .reset_index()
)
annual = annual[annual.year >= BASELINE_YEARS[0]]
n_members = annual.groupby("experiment").member.nunique()

# The baseline is the ensemble median of each run's 1950-2014 mean.
baseline_by_run = annual.query(
    "experiment == 'historical' and year <= @BASELINE_YEARS[1]"
).groupby("member").days.mean()
baseline_days = float(baseline_by_run.median())

rows = []
for scenario in SCENARIOS:
    runs = annual[annual.experiment == scenario]
    for period, (start, end) in FUTURE_PERIODS.items():
        by_run = runs[runs.year.between(start, end)].groupby("member").days.mean()
        low, high = np.percentile(by_run, SPREAD_PERCENTILES)
        median = float(by_run.median())
        rows.append({
            "scenario": scenario, "period": period, "median": median,
            "low": low, "high": high, "change": median - baseline_days,
            "change_pct": 100 * (median - baseline_days) / baseline_days,
        })
proj = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(["scenario", "period"])


def projected(scenario, period, column="median"):
    return proj.loc[(scenario, period), column]
```

The extract holds the 1° grid cell centered on `{python} f"{abs(cell_lat):.1f}"`° S, `{python} f"{abs(cell_lon):.1f}"`° W, which covers the city.
It contains every run in the Atlas ensemble: `{python} n_members["historical"]` historical runs and `{python} n_members[SCENARIOS].min()` to `{python} n_members[SCENARIOS].max()` runs per scenario.
The code sums each run's monthly counts into annual totals, then takes the median across runs.
The median resists the few models that run far hotter or cooler than the rest, and the band shows how far they spread.

```{python}
#| label: fig-climate
#| fig-cap: "Days per year above 35 °C in Pergamino's grid cell, one panel per emissions scenario. Lines show the ensemble median of each run's running mean; shaded bands show the spread across runs. Horizontal segments mark the median of each future period. Source: IPCC WGI Atlas, CMIP6, via the Copernicus Climate Data Store."
#| fig-alt: "Three line charts side by side, one each for SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5. Each shows a gray historical line near the baseline from 1950 to 2014, then a colored scenario line with a wide shaded band of model spread. The low and intermediate scenarios rise moderately and level off, while the high-emissions scenario climbs steeply toward 2100. Short black segments with numbers mark the median for 2020 to 2050, 2050 to 2070, and 2070 to 2100."
def ensemble_band(experiment):
    """Median and spread across runs of each run's smoothed annual count."""
    wide = annual[annual.experiment == experiment].pivot(
        index="year", columns="member", values="days"
    )
    smooth = wide.rolling(SMOOTH_YEARS, center=True, min_periods=SMOOTH_YEARS // 2 + 1).mean()
    low, high = np.nanpercentile(smooth, SPREAD_PERCENTILES, axis=1)
    return smooth.index.to_numpy(), smooth.median(axis=1).to_numpy(), low, high


bands = {e: ensemble_band(e) for e in ["historical", *SCENARIOS]}
high_ratio = projected("ssp585", "2070-2100") / baseline_days

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 4.4), sharey=True)
for ax, scenario in zip(axes, SCENARIOS, strict=True):
    for experiment in ["historical", scenario]:
        color = plot.SCENARIO_COLORS[experiment]
        years, median, low, high = bands[experiment]
        ax.fill_between(years, low, high, color=color, alpha=0.16, linewidth=0, zorder=1)
        ax.plot(years, median, color=color, lw=2, zorder=3)
    ax.axhline(baseline_days, color=plot.MUTED, lw=0.9, zorder=2)
    for period, (start, end) in FUTURE_PERIODS.items():
        value = projected(scenario, period)
        ax.hlines(value, start, end, color=plot.INK, lw=1.2, zorder=4)
        ax.text((start + end) / 2, value + 3, f"{value:.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom",
                fontsize=8.5, color=plot.INK, zorder=5,
                bbox={"boxstyle": "round,pad=0.15", "fc": "white", "ec": "none", "alpha": 0.8})
    ax.set_title(plot.SCENARIO_LABELS[scenario])
    ax.set_xlim(1950, 2100)
    ax.set_xticks([1950, 2000, 2050, 2100])
    ax.grid(axis="y")
    ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
    ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
axes[0].set_ylim(0, None)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Days per year above 35 °C")
axes[0].text(1952, baseline_days - 2.5, f"Baseline {baseline_days:.0f}", fontsize=8.5,
             color=plot.INK_SECONDARY, va="top")
lo_pct, hi_pct = SPREAD_PERCENTILES
handles = [
    plot.legend_line(plot.SCENARIO_COLORS["historical"], "Historical runs, median", 2),
    plot.legend_patch(plot.SCENARIO_COLORS["historical"],
                      f"{lo_pct}th to {hi_pct}th percentile of runs", 0.25),
    plot.legend_line(plot.INK, "Median of a future period", 1.2),
    plot.legend_line(plot.MUTED, "1950–2014 baseline", 0.9),
]
fig.legend(handles=handles, loc="outside lower center", ncols=4, fontsize=8)
plot.suptitle(
    fig,
    f"Hot days reach {high_ratio:.1f} times the baseline under SSP5-8.5",
)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-projections
#| tbl-cap: "Median days per year above 35 °C across model runs, with the spread across runs and the change from the 1950–2014 baseline."
table = proj.reset_index().assign(
    Scenario=lambda d: d.scenario.map(plot.SCENARIO_LABELS),
    Period=lambda d: d.period.str.replace("-", "–"),
    Days=lambda d: d["median"].round(0),
    Spread=lambda d: [f"{a:.0f}–{b:.0f}" for a, b in zip(d.low, d.high, strict=True)],
    Change=lambda d: [f"{c:+.0f} ({p:+.0f}%)" for c, p in zip(d.change, d.change_pct, strict=True)],
)[["Scenario", "Period", "Days", "Spread", "Change"]]
table.columns = [
    "Scenario", "Period", "Median days",
    f"{lo_pct}th–{hi_pct}th percentile of runs", "Change from baseline",
]
md_table(table, floatfmt="{:.0f}")
```

From 1950 to 2014, the median model run counts `{python} f"{baseline_days:.0f}"` days above 35 °C a year in Pergamino's grid cell.
Under the intermediate scenario, SSP2-4.5, the median rises to `{python} f"{projected('ssp245', '2020-2050'):.0f}"` days for 2020–2050, `{python} f"{projected('ssp245', '2050-2070'):.0f}"` for 2050–2070, and `{python} f"{projected('ssp245', '2070-2100'):.0f}"` for 2070–2100.
Even the low-emissions path adds `{python} f"{projected('ssp126', '2070-2100', 'change'):.0f}"` days a year by the end of the century.
The high-emissions path adds `{python} f"{projected('ssp585', '2070-2100', 'change'):.0f}"`.

The spread between runs is wide.
For 2070–2100 under SSP2-4.5, the middle 80% of runs range from `{python} f"{projected('ssp245', '2070-2100', 'low'):.0f}"` to `{python} f"{projected('ssp245', '2070-2100', 'high'):.0f}"` days.
That range is a reason to plan for several futures at once, which the [recommendations](#recommendations) do.

## Current heat patterns: where is it hottest now?

The projections say how much heat is coming.
The next question is where, inside the city, it lands hardest.
This section moves from a 1° climate grid, about 100 km across, to a 30 m satellite grid that resolves single blocks and parks.

The [P95 land surface temperature composite](https://source.coop/nlebovits/landsat-lst) takes the upper percentile, P95, of every clear Landsat 8 and 9 observation from 2021 through 2025.
Before the percentile, the pipeline removes each scene's bulk offset from its monthly normal, then blends overlapping orbital paths to remove stripes.
The [repository README](https://github.com/nlebovits/landsat-lst-pipeline#data-processing-storage-and-access) describes both steps, and the STAC item's `processing:lineage` field records them for each tile.
The result shows where the ground runs hottest on hot days, relative to its surroundings.

::: {.callout-important}
## Surface temperature is not air temperature

Land surface temperature measures how hot the ground and roofs get, not the air a person breathes.
On a hot afternoon, a dark roof can run 20 °C or more above the air around it.
Read the composite as a relative indicator that ranks places by how much heat their ground and roofs absorb.
It does not predict the heat stress a person feels.
:::

The tile `S30W065` covers 5° by 5°, far more than Pergamino needs.
`rasterio` reads only the window over the partido, plus the matching window of `qa_count`, the per-month count of clear observations behind each percentile.

```{python}
#| label: lst
item = pystac.Item.from_file(LST_ITEM_URL)
band = item.assets["lst_p95"].extra_fields["bands"][0]
LST_SCALE, LST_OFFSET = band["raster:scale"], band["raster:offset"]

# The analysis grid is the LST grid, cut to the partido plus about 1 km.
pad = 0.01
px0, py0, px1, py1 = partido.total_bounds
AOI_BOUNDS = (px0 - pad, py0 - pad, px1 + pad, py1 + pad)

with rasterio.Env(**GDAL_ENV):
    with rasterio.open(item.assets["lst_p95"].get_absolute_href()) as src:
        window = from_bounds(*AOI_BOUNDS, transform=src.transform)
        window = window.round_offsets().round_lengths()
        GRID_TRANSFORM = src.window_transform(window)
        GRID_CRS = src.crs
        lst_dn = src.read(1, window=window)
    with rasterio.open(item.assets["qa_count"].get_absolute_href()) as src:
        qa_monthly = src.read(window=window)
GRID_SHAPE = lst_dn.shape
GRID_EXTENT = (
    GRID_TRANSFORM.c,
    GRID_TRANSFORM.c + GRID_TRANSFORM.a * GRID_SHAPE[1],
    GRID_TRANSFORM.f + GRID_TRANSFORM.e * GRID_SHAPE[0],
    GRID_TRANSFORM.f,
)
lst = np.where(lst_dn == 0, np.nan, lst_dn * LST_SCALE + LST_OFFSET).astype("float32")
qa_total = qa_monthly.sum(axis=0, dtype="int32")

# A pixel on a geographic grid shrinks east-west with latitude. Its area, in
# square metres, spreads a census count over a tract that has no modeled
# population.
lat_centres = GRID_TRANSFORM.f + (np.arange(GRID_SHAPE[0]) + 0.5) * GRID_TRANSFORM.e
pixel_w_m = abs(GRID_TRANSFORM.a) * plot.METRES_PER_DEGREE * np.cos(np.radians(lat_centres))
pixel_h_m = abs(GRID_TRANSFORM.e) * plot.METRES_PER_DEGREE
PIXEL_AREA_M2 = np.repeat((pixel_w_m * pixel_h_m)[:, None], GRID_SHAPE[1], axis=1)


def burn(shapes, dtype="uint8"):
    """Rasterize (geometry, value) pairs onto the analysis grid, by pixel centre."""
    return rasterize(shapes, out_shape=GRID_SHAPE, transform=GRID_TRANSFORM, fill=0, dtype=dtype)


def grid_window(bounds):
    """The window of the analysis grid that covers bounds, rounded outward."""
    win = from_bounds(*bounds, transform=GRID_TRANSFORM)
    c0, r0 = math.floor(win.col_off), math.floor(win.row_off)
    c1 = math.ceil(win.col_off + win.width)
    r1 = math.ceil(win.row_off + win.height)
    return Window(c0, r0, c1 - c0, r1 - r0)


class_codes = {name: i + 1 for i, name in enumerate(URBAN_CLASSES)}
urban_class = burn(
    (g, class_codes[c])
    for g, c in zip(aglomerados.geometry, aglomerados.clasificacion, strict=True)
)
in_urban = urban_class > 0
in_partido = burn([(partido.geometry.iloc[0], 1)]).astype(bool)
min_obs_urban = int(qa_total[in_urban].min())
median_obs_urban = float(np.median(qa_total[in_urban]))
lst_partido_median = float(np.nanmedian(lst[in_partido]))
lst_class_median = {c: float(np.nanmedian(lst[urban_class == class_codes[c]])) for c in URBAN_CLASSES}
```

The read fetches part of a `{python} f"{item.assets['lst_p95'].extra_fields['file:size'] / 1e6:.0f}"` MB file.
The window holds `{python} f"{GRID_SHAPE[0]:,} × {GRID_SHAPE[1]:,}"` pixels, each about `{python} f"{pixel_w_m.mean():.0f}"` m wide and `{python} f"{pixel_h_m:.0f}"` m tall at this latitude.
Every pixel inside the urban classes has a value.
The thinnest evidence behind any of them is `{python} min_obs_urban` clear observations, and the median is `{python} f"{median_obs_urban:.0f}"`.
The product requires at least five.

### Hotspots by urban class

One threshold for the whole partido would flag mostly farmland.
The median pixel in the partido reaches `{python} f"{lst_partido_median:.1f}"` °C, against `{python} f"{lst_class_median['urbana']:.1f}"` °C in the city.
Bare fields after harvest run hotter than most streets, and they have almost no residents.
The question here is where heat and people meet.

For that reason, the analysis sets one threshold per urban class: the `{python} HOTSPOT_PERCENTILE`th percentile of that class's own pixels.
A hotspot in the urban core and a hotspot in a rural town can differ by a degree or more, yet each marks the hottest `{python} 100 - HOTSPOT_PERCENTILE`% of its own setting.
Treat this rule as a heuristic, and check it against what local staff know about each place.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-classes
#| tbl-cap: "Surface temperature and hotspot thresholds by urban class."
thresholds = {}
hotspot = np.zeros(GRID_SHAPE, dtype=bool)
for name, code in class_codes.items():
    in_class = (urban_class == code) & np.isfinite(lst)
    thresholds[name] = float(np.percentile(lst[in_class], HOTSPOT_PERCENTILE))
    hotspot |= in_class & (lst >= thresholds[name])

table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Urban class": [plot.URBAN_CLASS_LABELS[c] for c in URBAN_CLASSES],
    "Area (km²)": class_area_km2.to_numpy(),
    "Median P95 LST (°C)": [lst_class_median[c] for c in URBAN_CLASSES],
    "Hotspot threshold (°C)": [thresholds[c] for c in URBAN_CLASSES],
    "Median clear observations": [
        float(np.median(qa_total[urban_class == class_codes[c]])) for c in URBAN_CLASSES
    ],
})
md_table(table)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-lst
#| fig-cap: "Left, the 95th percentile land surface temperature for 2021–2025 around the city of Pergamino, with the urban and peri-urban classes outlined in white. Right, the number of clear observations behind each pixel. Source: Landsat LST P95 composite on Source Cooperative."
#| fig-alt: "Two maps of the city of Pergamino. The left map uses a dark purple to pale yellow scale for temperature. The built-up core and the river corridor appear dark and cool, while surrounding fields and open lots at the city's edge appear bright and hot. The right map shows observation counts, lowest in the city center and highest toward the west."
def stepped_norm(values, step, cmap):
    """A color scale in fixed steps spanning the 2nd to 98th percentile."""
    lo, hi = np.nanpercentile(values, [2, 98])
    edges = np.arange(np.floor(lo / step) * step, np.ceil(hi / step) * step + step / 2, step)
    return BoundaryNorm(edges, plt.get_cmap(cmap).N, extend="both")


city_win = grid_window(city_frame)
city_rows, city_cols = city_win.toslices()
in_city_frame = np.zeros(GRID_SHAPE, dtype=bool)
in_city_frame[city_rows, city_cols] = True
lst_norm = stepped_norm(lst[in_city_frame], 0.5, plot.CMAP_LST)
obs_norm = stepped_norm(qa_total[in_city_frame], 20, plot.CMAP_OBSERVATIONS)

fig, (ax_l, ax_q) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.9))
im = ax_l.imshow(lst, extent=GRID_EXTENT, cmap=plot.CMAP_LST, norm=lst_norm, zorder=1)
qm = ax_q.imshow(qa_total, extent=GRID_EXTENT, cmap=plot.CMAP_OBSERVATIONS, norm=obs_norm,
                 zorder=1)
for ax in (ax_l, ax_q):
    plot.frame(ax, city_frame, margin=0.01)
    city_outline.plot(ax=ax, color="white", linewidth=0.7, zorder=3)
    plot.scalebar(ax)
plot.north_arrow(ax_q)
plot.colorbar_below(ax_l, im, "95th percentile land surface temperature (°C)",
                    ticks=lst_norm.boundaries[::2], extend="both")
plot.colorbar_below(ax_q, qm, "Clear observations behind the percentile, 2021–2025",
                    ticks=obs_norm.boundaries[::2], extend="both")
ax_l.set_title("Hot-season surface temperature")
ax_q.set_title("Evidence behind each pixel")
plot.suptitle(fig, "Open ground around the city runs hotter than the built-up core")
plt.show()
```

The built-up core and the tree-lined Arroyo Pergamino run coolest.
Fields and open lots outside the city show the highest values in the frame.
Inside the urban classes, the hottest pixels line the city's fringe, where new subdivisions, vacant lots, and industrial yards leave ground exposed.

The core also has the fewest clear observations.
Every pixel there still has many times the five-observation minimum, enough for a stable percentile.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hotspots
#| fig-cap: "Hotspots, the pixels hotter than their class's threshold, over greyscale imagery. One panel each for the urban and peri-urban classes, and one for each of the two largest rural settlements. Source: Landsat LST P95 composite; Municipalidad de Pergamino; imagery from Esri."
#| fig-alt: "Four maps. The large left map shows the urban class in light blue with magenta hotspot patches concentrated along the city's northern, eastern and southern edges and a few in the interior. A top-right map shows small orange peri-urban patches around the city, many partly magenta. Two small bottom-right maps show rural towns in green with magenta hotspot patches on their edges."
def square_bounds(geom_projected, side_m):
    """Degree bounds of a square, at least side_m wide, centred on a geometry."""
    x0, y0, x1, y1 = geom_projected.bounds
    cx, cy = (x0 + x1) / 2, (y0 + y1) / 2
    half = max(side_m, x1 - x0, y1 - y0) * 0.55
    square = gpd.GeoSeries([box(cx - half, cy - half, cx + half, cy + half)], crs=AREA_CRS)
    return square.to_crs("EPSG:4326").total_bounds


def hotspot_panel(ax, name, bounds, title, margin=0.02):
    code = class_codes[name]
    plot.frame(ax, bounds, margin=margin)
    plot.basemap(ax, dim=0.45, credit=False)
    in_class = np.where(urban_class == code, 1.0, np.nan)
    hot = np.where(hotspot & (urban_class == code), 1.0, np.nan)
    ax.imshow(in_class, extent=GRID_EXTENT, alpha=0.4, zorder=1,
              cmap=plot.single_color_cmap(plot.URBAN_CLASS_COLORS[name]))
    ax.imshow(hot, extent=GRID_EXTENT, zorder=2, cmap=plot.single_color_cmap(plot.HOTSPOT_COLOR))
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9.5)
    plot.scalebar(ax)


rural = aglomerados[aglomerados.clasificacion == "urbano en ruralidad"]
largest_towns = (
    rural.to_crs(AREA_CRS)
    .assign(area=lambda d: d.area)
    .dissolve("distrito", aggfunc="sum")
    .sort_values("area", ascending=False)
    .head(RURAL_PANELS)
)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6.4))
grid = fig.add_gridspec(2, 2 + RURAL_PANELS)
ax_u = fig.add_subplot(grid[:, 0:2])
hotspot_panel(ax_u, "urbana", city[city.clasificacion == "urbana"].total_bounds,
              f"Urban, threshold {thresholds['urbana']:.1f} °C")
ax_pu = fig.add_subplot(grid[0, 2:])
hotspot_panel(ax_pu, "periurbana", city_frame,
              f"Peri-urban, threshold {thresholds['periurbana']:.1f} °C")
for i, (town, row) in enumerate(largest_towns.iterrows()):
    ax = fig.add_subplot(grid[1, 2 + i])
    hotspot_panel(ax, "urbano en ruralidad", square_bounds(row.geometry, 3000),
                  f"{town}, rural, {thresholds['urbano en ruralidad']:.1f} °C", margin=0)
plot.north_arrow(ax_u)
handles = [
    plot.legend_patch(plot.HOTSPOT_COLOR, f"Hotspot: hottest {100 - HOTSPOT_PERCENTILE}% of its class"),
    *[
        plot.legend_patch(c, f"{plot.URBAN_CLASS_LABELS[k]}, below threshold", 0.5)
        for k, c in plot.URBAN_CLASS_COLORS.items()
    ],
]
fig.legend(handles=handles, loc="outside lower center", ncols=4, fontsize=8)
plot.suptitle(fig, "Most hotspots sit on the edges of built-up land")
plt.show()
```

## What drives the heat

A hotspot map shows where to act.
Canopy and buildings suggest what to do there.
Shade from trees cools the ground beneath it, while a roof's temperature depends on its material and color.
This section measures both at the scale of the LST pixel.

- **Canopy cover** is the share of each pixel where the [Meta and WRI canopy height model](https://source.coop/tge-labs/meta-chm-v2) reports trees at least `{python} CANOPY_HEIGHT_M` m tall. The model maps height at 1.19 m, which gives several hundred canopy cells per LST pixel.
- **Building cover** is the share of each pixel under an [Overture Maps](https://docs.overturemaps.org/guides/buildings/) building footprint.

Both layers come from global, openly licensed sources, which lets you repeat the analysis in any city.
The code reads them only inside the urban classes.
Each separate piece of urban land becomes one small window, which keeps the rural settlements from pulling in the whole partido.

```{python}
#| label: buildings
overture_release = OVERTURE_RELEASE

# Filter on the bounding box of the urban classes in DuckDB, then clip locally.
ux0, uy0, ux1, uy1 = aglomerados.total_bounds
buildings = read_geoparquet(f"""
    SELECT id, ST_AsWKB(geometry) AS geometry
    FROM read_parquet('s3://overturemaps-us-west-2/release/{overture_release}/theme=buildings/type=building/*.parquet')
    WHERE bbox.xmin <= {ux1} AND bbox.xmax >= {ux0}
      AND bbox.ymin <= {uy1} AND bbox.ymax >= {uy0}
""")
buildings = buildings[buildings.intersects(aglomerados.union_all())].reset_index(drop=True)
```

```{python}
#| label: cover
WEB_MERCATOR_ORIGIN = -20037508.342789244

chm_tiles = con.sql(f"""
    SELECT quadkey, cog_url
    FROM '{CHM_TILES_URL}'
    WHERE bbox.xmin <= {ux1} AND bbox.xmax >= {ux0}
      AND bbox.ymin <= {uy1} AND bbox.ymax >= {uy0}
""").df()

# One window per separate piece of urban land, grown by 60 m.
pieces = aglomerados.to_crs(AREA_CRS).buffer(60).union_all()
pieces = gpd.GeoSeries(list(pieces.geoms), crs=AREA_CRS).to_crs("EPSG:4326")


def building_cover(win):
    """Share of each pixel in win under a building footprint."""
    fine = rasterio.windows.transform(win, GRID_TRANSFORM) * Affine.scale(1 / SUPERSAMPLE)
    bounds = rasterio.windows.bounds(win, GRID_TRANSFORM)
    footprints = buildings.geometry[buildings.intersects(box(*bounds))]
    if footprints.empty:
        return np.zeros((win.height, win.width), dtype="float32")
    shape = (win.height * SUPERSAMPLE, win.width * SUPERSAMPLE)
    mask = rasterize(footprints, out_shape=shape, transform=fine, fill=0, dtype="uint8")
    return mask.reshape(win.height, SUPERSAMPLE, win.width, SUPERSAMPLE).mean(axis=(1, 3))


def canopy_cover(win, sources):
    """Share of each pixel in win with canopy at least CANOPY_HEIGHT_M tall."""
    bounds = rasterio.windows.bounds(win, GRID_TRANSFORM)
    x0, y0, x1, y1 = transform_bounds("EPSG:4326", "EPSG:3857", *bounds)
    res = sources[0].res[0]
    # The canopy tiles share one global Web Mercator pixel grid, which turns
    # a mosaic of several tiles into array slicing.
    c0 = math.floor((x0 - WEB_MERCATOR_ORIGIN) / res)
    r0 = math.floor((-WEB_MERCATOR_ORIGIN - y1) / res)
    c1 = math.ceil((x1 - WEB_MERCATOR_ORIGIN) / res)
    r1 = math.ceil((-WEB_MERCATOR_ORIGIN - y0) / res)
    mosaic = np.full((r1 - r0, c1 - c0), np.nan, dtype="float32")
    for src in sources:
        tc = round((src.transform.c - WEB_MERCATOR_ORIGIN) / res)
        tr = round((-WEB_MERCATOR_ORIGIN - src.transform.f) / res)
        cc0, rr0 = max(c0, tc), max(r0, tr)
        cc1, rr1 = min(c1, tc + src.width), min(r1, tr + src.height)
        if cc0 >= cc1 or rr0 >= rr1:
            continue
        heights = src.read(1, window=Window(cc0 - tc, rr0 - tr, cc1 - cc0, rr1 - rr0))
        mosaic[rr0 - r0 : rr1 - r0, cc0 - c0 : cc1 - c0] = heights >= CANOPY_HEIGHT_M
    out = np.full((win.height, win.width), np.nan, dtype="float32")
    origin = Affine(res, 0, WEB_MERCATOR_ORIGIN + c0 * res, 0, -res, -WEB_MERCATOR_ORIGIN - r0 * res)
    reproject(
        mosaic, out,
        src_transform=origin, src_crs="EPSG:3857", src_nodata=np.nan,
        dst_transform=rasterio.windows.transform(win, GRID_TRANSFORM), dst_crs=GRID_CRS,
        dst_nodata=np.nan, resampling=Resampling.average,
    )
    return out


building_share = np.full(GRID_SHAPE, np.nan, dtype="float32")
canopy_share = np.full(GRID_SHAPE, np.nan, dtype="float32")
with rasterio.Env(**GDAL_ENV):
    sources = [rasterio.open(url) for url in chm_tiles.cog_url]
    chm_tile_px = sources[0].width
    try:
        for piece in pieces:
            win = grid_window(piece.bounds)
            rows, cols = win.toslices()
            building_share[rows, cols] = building_cover(win)
            canopy_share[rows, cols] = canopy_cover(win, sources)
    finally:
        for src in sources:
            src.close()
building_share[~in_urban] = np.nan
canopy_share[~in_urban] = np.nan
```

The urban classes span `{python} len(chm_tiles)` canopy tiles, each a COG `{python} f"{chm_tile_px:,}"` pixels on a side.
The code reads `{python} len(pieces)` small windows from them rather than the tiles themselves.
DuckDB returns `{python} n(len(buildings))` buildings inside the urban classes from Overture release `{python} overture_release`.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cover
#| fig-cap: "Canopy cover, left, and building footprint cover, right, inside Pergamino's urban and peri-urban classes. Each square averages a block of LST pixels, set by `DISPLAY_BLOCK`. Sources: Meta and WRI canopy height model v2; Overture Maps buildings; imagery from Esri."
#| fig-alt: "Two maps of the city. The left map shades canopy cover in greens, patchy across the city with the darkest greens in small areas on the fringe and in parks. The right map shades building cover in purples, darkest in a compact block at the city center and fading toward the edges."
def block_mean(values, win, k=DISPLAY_BLOCK):
    """Mean of each k by k block inside win, ignoring NaN, with its plot extent."""
    rows, cols = win.toslices()
    sub = values[rows, cols]
    h, w = (sub.shape[0] // k) * k, (sub.shape[1] // k) * k
    out = np.nanmean(sub[:h, :w].reshape(h // k, k, w // k, k), axis=(1, 3))
    left, top = GRID_TRANSFORM * (win.col_off, win.row_off)
    right, bottom = GRID_TRANSFORM * (win.col_off + w, win.row_off + h)
    return out, (left, right, bottom, top)


def truncated(cmap, start=0.12):
    """A sequential colormap whose lowest value is a visible tint, not white."""
    base = plt.get_cmap(cmap)
    return LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list(f"{cmap}_t", base(np.linspace(start, 1, 256)))


cover_norm = BoundaryNorm(np.arange(0, 60, 10), 256, extend="max")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.9))
for ax, share, cmap, label, title in [
    (axes[0], canopy_share, plot.CMAP_CANOPY,
     f"Canopy at least {CANOPY_HEIGHT_M} m tall (% of area)", "Tree canopy"),
    (axes[1], building_share, plot.CMAP_BUILDINGS, "Building footprint (% of area)", "Buildings"),
]:
    plot.frame(ax, city_frame, margin=0.01)
    plot.basemap(ax, dim=0.6, credit=ax is axes[1])
    blocks, extent = block_mean(100 * share, city_win)
    im = ax.imshow(blocks, extent=extent, cmap=truncated(cmap), norm=cover_norm, zorder=1)
    city_outline.plot(ax=ax, color=plot.INK, linewidth=0.5, zorder=3)
    plot.scalebar(ax)
    plot.colorbar_below(ax, im, label, ticks=cover_norm.boundaries)
    ax.set_title(title)
plot.north_arrow(axes[1])
plot.suptitle(fig, "Buildings fill the core and canopy clusters near the edge")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: drivers
valid = in_urban & np.isfinite(lst) & np.isfinite(canopy_share)
drivers = pd.DataFrame({
    "lst": lst[valid],
    "canopy": 100 * canopy_share[valid],
    "buildings": 100 * building_share[valid],
})


def median_lst(column, lo, hi):
    """Median LST of pixels whose cover lies in [lo, hi) percent."""
    return float(drivers.lst[(drivers[column] >= lo) & (drivers[column] < hi)].median())


bare = (drivers.canopy < 5) & (drivers.buildings < 5)
bare_share = 100 * bare.mean()
bare_lst = float(drivers.lst[bare].median())
covered_lst = float(drivers.lst[~bare].median())
canopy_low, canopy_high = median_lst("canopy", 0, 5), median_lst("canopy", 30, 101)
roof_mid, roof_full = median_lst("buildings", 30, 70), median_lst("buildings", 90, 101)
rho = drivers.corr(method="spearman")

# One least-squares fit with both covers, in °C per 10 percentage points.
design = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(drivers)), drivers.canopy / 10, drivers.buildings / 10])
coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(design, drivers.lst, rcond=None)
residual = drivers.lst - design @ coef
r2 = 1 - (residual**2).sum() / ((drivers.lst - drivers.lst.mean()) ** 2).sum()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-drivers
#| fig-cap: "Each urban pixel's 95th percentile LST against its canopy cover, left, and building cover, right. Gray hexagons count pixels on a log scale; colored lines join the median LST of each bin of cover with enough pixels for a stable median. Sources: Landsat LST P95 composite; Meta and WRI canopy height model v2; Overture Maps buildings."
#| fig-alt: "Two hexbin scatter plots with temperature on the vertical axis. In both, a dense column of pixels sits at zero cover. The green canopy line drops by about a degree from zero cover to a few percent, then declines slowly. The purple building line also drops from zero cover, flattens across the middle, and rises again above about 80 percent cover."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.6), sharey=True)
lst_lo, lst_hi = np.percentile(drivers.lst, [0.5, 99.5])
handles = []
for ax, column, cmap, label in [
    (axes[0], "canopy", plot.CMAP_CANOPY, f"Canopy at least {CANOPY_HEIGHT_M} m tall (% of pixel)"),
    (axes[1], "buildings", plot.CMAP_BUILDINGS, "Building footprint (% of pixel)"),
]:
    hb = ax.hexbin(drivers[column], drivers.lst, gridsize=(40, 30),
                   extent=(0, 100, lst_lo, lst_hi), cmap=truncated("Greys", 0.08),
                   norm=LogNorm(), mincnt=1, linewidths=0.2, edgecolors="face", zorder=1)
    bins = np.arange(0, 100 + BIN_WIDTH, BIN_WIDTH)
    grouped = drivers.groupby(pd.cut(drivers[column], bins, include_lowest=True), observed=True)
    stats = grouped.lst.agg(["median", "size"]).query("size >= @MIN_BIN_PIXELS")
    centres = np.array([iv.mid for iv in stats.index])
    color = plt.get_cmap(cmap)(0.8)
    ax.plot(centres, stats["median"], color=color, lw=2, zorder=3)
    ax.scatter(centres, stats["median"], s=22, color=color, edgecolor="white", lw=1, zorder=4)
    handles.append(plot.legend_line(color, f"Median LST per {BIN_WIDTH}-point bin of {column}", 2))
    ax.set_xlabel(label)
    ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
    ax.grid(axis="y")
axes[0].set_ylabel("95th percentile LST (°C)")
axes[0].set_ylim(lst_lo, lst_hi)
bar = fig.colorbar(hb, ax=axes, orientation="vertical", fraction=0.025, pad=0.01)
bar.outline.set_visible(False)
bar.set_label("Pixels per hexagon", fontsize=8.5)
bar.ax.tick_params(labelsize=8, length=2)
fig.legend(handles=handles, loc="outside lower center", ncols=2, fontsize=8)
plot.suptitle(fig, "Bare pixels run hottest")
plt.show()
```

The clearest signal is between bare and covered ground.
Pixels with less than 5% canopy and less than 5% building cover make up `{python} f"{bare_share:.0f}"`% of urban land.
Their median reaches `{python} f"{bare_lst:.1f}"` °C, against `{python} f"{covered_lst:.1f}"` °C for the rest.
Pixels with at least 30% canopy run at a median of `{python} f"{canopy_high:.1f}"` °C, compared with `{python} f"{canopy_low:.1f}"` °C below 5%.

Buildings behave differently from what the term urban heat island suggests.
At P95, a mix of roofs, streets, and yards runs cooler than open ground, with a median of `{python} f"{roof_mid:.1f}"` °C at 30% to 70% building cover.
Pixels almost entirely under roof heat up again, to `{python} f"{roof_full:.1f}"` °C above 90% cover.
Those pixels are mostly large industrial and commercial sheds.

A linear fit with both covers explains `{python} f"{100 * r2:.0f}"`% of the variation in LST.
Each 10 points of canopy goes with `{python} f"{coef[1]:+.2f}"` °C, holding building cover fixed, and each 10 points of building cover with `{python} f"{coef[2]:+.2f}"` °C.
These coefficients describe associations across pixels, and planting a tree in one spot may change LST by more or less.
Soil moisture, irrigation, and surface materials vary with both covers, and neighboring pixels share their heat.

## Exposure: who lives in hot areas?

Each population source has its own errors.
This section compares three, and reports how far they disagree instead of one number:

- **[GHS-POP R2023A](https://human-settlement.emergency.copernicus.eu/ghs_pop2023.php)** models residential population on a 100 m grid worldwide. The 2025 epoch projects forward from earlier inputs, and the model disaggregates national totals using detected built-up area.
- **The [2022 census](https://www.indec.gob.ar/indec/web/Nivel4-Tema-2-41-165)** counts people by census tract, called a *radio censal*. INDEC publishes the official figure that municipalities plan with, but every census misses some people, and tracts are coarse.
- **[Overture building footprints](https://docs.overturemaps.org/guides/buildings/)** say where structures stand. They count no people, but they check where the other two sources put them.

The [GHSL mirror](https://source.coop/nlebovits/ghsl) indexes its tiles in a STAC GeoParquet file.
The code finds the tiles that cover the partido and reads one window from each in its native Mollweide projection.
It then moves the counts onto the LST grid with [sum resampling](https://gdal.org/en/stable/programs/gdalwarp.html#cmdoption-gdalwarp-r).
GDAL splits each 100 m cell's count among the LST pixels that overlap it, in proportion to the overlap, which keeps the total.

```{python}
#| label: ghsl
x0, y0, x1, y1 = AOI_BOUNDS
ghsl_items = con.sql(f"""
    SELECT id, assets.data.href AS href, "proj:bbox" AS proj_bbox
    FROM '{GHSL_ITEMS_URL}'
    WHERE bbox.xmin <= {x1} AND bbox.xmax >= {x0} AND bbox.ymin <= {y1} AND bbox.ymax >= {y0}
""").df()

# STAC bboxes are generous on a curved grid. Keep the items whose native
# Mollweide extent overlaps the area, and read only that window.
GHSL_CRS = "ESRI:54009"
mx0, my0, mx1, my1 = transform_bounds("EPSG:4326", GHSL_CRS, *AOI_BOUNDS, densify_pts=21)
partido_native = partido.to_crs(GHSL_CRS).geometry.iloc[0]
ghsl_native_partido = 0.0  # the partido's total on the native grid, for a check
ghsl_pop = np.zeros(GRID_SHAPE, dtype="float32")  # persons per LST pixel
with rasterio.Env(**GDAL_ENV):
    for row in ghsl_items.itertuples():
        bx0, by0, bx1, by1 = row.proj_bbox
        if bx0 > mx1 or bx1 < mx0 or by0 > my1 or by1 < my0:
            continue
        # The asset href is relative to its item, which sits in a folder named by id.
        url = f"{GHSL_ITEMS_URL.rsplit('/', 1)[0]}/{row.id}/{row.href.removeprefix('./')}"
        with rasterio.open(url) as src:
            win = from_bounds(mx0, my0, mx1, my1, transform=src.transform)
            win = win.round_offsets().round_lengths()
            people = src.read(1, window=win, boundless=True, fill_value=0)
            people = np.where(people < 0, 0, people).astype("float32")  # nodata is negative
            native_in_partido = rasterize(
                [(partido_native, 1)], out_shape=people.shape,
                transform=src.window_transform(win), fill=0, dtype="uint8",
            )
            ghsl_native_partido += float(people[native_in_partido == 1].sum())
            # Sum resampling moves counts, not densities. Each LST pixel gets
            # the overlap-weighted share of every 100 m cell it touches.
            part = np.zeros(GRID_SHAPE, dtype="float32")
            reproject(
                people, part,
                src_transform=src.window_transform(win), src_crs=src.crs, src_nodata=-1,
                dst_transform=GRID_TRANSFORM, dst_crs=GRID_CRS, dst_nodata=0,
                resampling=Resampling.sum,
            )
            ghsl_pop += part
```

On its native grid, GHS-POP places `{python} n(ghsl_native_partido)` people in the partido, and the LST grid holds `{python} n(ghsl_pop[in_partido].sum())`.
Each grid assigns a cell on the partido boundary by its center, which accounts for the small difference.

The census joins two files from the [census catalog](https://source.coop/nlebovits/censo-argentino).
`radios.parquet` holds tract boundaries and total population, `POB_TOT_P`.
`census-data.parquet` holds tabulations in long form, one row per tract, variable, and category.
The query keeps tracts in Pergamino, coded province `06` and department `623`.

The code then spreads each tract's census count over the LST pixels inside it, in proportion to GHS-POP's modeled population there.
This dasymetric step keeps the census total while placing people where buildings stand.
A tract where GHS-POP models nobody spreads its count evenly over its area.

```{python}
#| label: census
deprived = ", ".join(f"'{c}'" for c in DEPRIVED_IPMH_CATEGORIES)
tracts = read_geoparquet(f"""
    WITH ipmh AS (
        SELECT
            id_geo,
            SUM(conteo) FILTER (WHERE valor_categoria IN ({deprived})) AS households_deprived,
            SUM(conteo) AS households
        FROM '{CENSUS_URL}/census-data.parquet'
        WHERE codigo_variable = 'HOGAR_IPMH'
          AND prov_code = 6 AND valor_departamento = '623'
        GROUP BY id_geo
    )
    SELECT
        r.COD_2022 AS tract,
        r.POB_TOT_P AS population,
        COALESCE(i.households_deprived, 0) AS households_deprived,
        COALESCE(i.households, 0) AS households,
        ST_AsWKB(r.geometry) AS geometry
    FROM '{CENSUS_URL}/radios.parquet' r
    LEFT JOIN ipmh i ON r.COD_2022 = i.id_geo
    WHERE r.PROV = '06' AND r.DEPTO = '623'
""")
tracts["deprived_share"] = (tracts.households_deprived / tracts.households).fillna(0.0)

tract_id = burn(((g, i + 1) for i, g in enumerate(tracts.geometry)), dtype="int32")
k = len(tracts) + 1
ghsl_by_tract = np.bincount(tract_id.ravel(), weights=ghsl_pop.ravel(), minlength=k)
area_by_tract = np.bincount(tract_id.ravel(), weights=PIXEL_AREA_M2.ravel(), minlength=k)
census_total = np.r_[0.0, tracts.population.to_numpy(dtype="float64")]
modelled = ghsl_by_tract > 0
weight = np.where(
    modelled[tract_id],
    ghsl_pop / np.where(modelled, ghsl_by_tract, 1.0)[tract_id],
    PIXEL_AREA_M2 / np.where(area_by_tract > 0, area_by_tract, 1.0)[tract_id],
)
census_pop = np.where(tract_id > 0, weight * census_total[tract_id], 0.0).astype("float32")
vulnerable_pop = census_pop * np.r_[0.0, tracts.deprived_share.to_numpy()][tract_id]
```

```{python}
#| label: exposure
# Count each building once, in the pixel that holds its representative point.
points = buildings.representative_point()
cols, rows = ~GRID_TRANSFORM * (points.x.to_numpy(), points.y.to_numpy())
building_count = np.zeros(GRID_SHAPE, dtype="int32")
np.add.at(building_count, (rows.astype(int), cols.astype(int)), 1)


def by_class(values):
    """Sum a per-pixel quantity within each urban class, and within its hotspots."""
    total = np.bincount(urban_class.ravel(), weights=values.ravel(), minlength=4)[1:]
    hot = np.bincount(urban_class.ravel(), weights=(values * hotspot).ravel(), minlength=4)[1:]
    return total, hot


SOURCE_UNITS = {"GHS-POP 2025": "people", "Census 2022": "people", "Overture buildings": "buildings"}
rows = []
for source, values in zip(SOURCE_UNITS, [ghsl_pop, census_pop, building_count], strict=True):
    total, hot = by_class(values)
    for name, t, h in zip(URBAN_CLASSES, total, hot, strict=True):
        rows.append({"source": source, "class": name, "total": t, "in_hotspots": h})
exposure = pd.DataFrame(rows).assign(share=lambda d: 100 * d.in_hotspots / d.total)

ghsl_partido = float(ghsl_pop[in_partido].sum())
census_partido = float(tracts.population.sum())
ghsl_urban = float(ghsl_pop[in_urban].sum())
census_urban = float(census_pop[in_urban].sum())
buildings_urban = int(building_count[in_urban].sum())
divergence = 100 * (ghsl_partido - census_partido) / census_partido
people_per_building = census_urban / buildings_urban
exposed = exposure.pivot(index="class", columns="source", values="in_hotspots").reindex(URBAN_CLASSES)
exposed_low = exposed[["GHS-POP 2025", "Census 2022"]].sum().min()
exposed_high = exposed[["GHS-POP 2025", "Census 2022"]].sum().max()
```

The census counts `{python} n(census_partido)` people in the partido in 2022.
GHS-POP models `{python} n(ghsl_partido)` for 2025, `{python} f"{divergence:+.0f}"`% from the census.
Inside the urban classes, the sources come closer: `{python} n(census_urban)` people by census and `{python} n(ghsl_urban)` by GHS-POP.
Overture places `{python} n(buildings_urban)` buildings there, about `{python} f"{people_per_building:.1f}"` census residents per building.

Several mechanisms explain a gap between modeled and counted population:

- **Time:** the 2025 epoch projects forward from earlier inputs, while the census records 2022.
- **Placement:** GHS-POP distributes people by detected built-up area, which can overfill industrial land and underfill dense blocks.
- **Undercount:** a census misses some people, most often in informal housing or among seasonal workers.

A gap above about 20% calls for a closer look, because it often points to something on the ground.
For rates, this tutorial uses the census figure, since the municipality plans with it, and reports the range across sources.

```{python}

The vertical line marks the share that an even spread across the class would put there. Sources: GHS-POP R2023A; INDEC census 2022; Overture Maps buildings; Landsat LST P95 composite."

Between `{python} n(exposed_low)` and `{python} n(exposed_high)` people live in hotspots, depending on the source.
Every class holds fewer people in its hotspots than an even spread would place there, because the hottest pixels are the emptiest ones.
That finding matches the driver analysis: bare lots, yards, and sheds heat up, and few people sleep in them.
The people who do live there sit on the city's growing edge, which makes them the focus of the next two sections.

```{python}
#| label: tracts-city
in_city = np.isin(urban_class, [class_codes["urbana"], class_codes["periurbana"]])


def per_tract(values):
    """Sum a per-pixel quantity over each census radio's urban and peri-urban land."""
    v = np.nan_to_num(values) * in_city
    return np.bincount(tract_id.ravel(), weights=v.ravel(), minlength=len(tracts) + 1)[1:]


# Each census radio, cut to the city's urban and peri-urban classes.
city_tracts = tracts.assign(
    residents=per_tract(census_pop),
    exposed=per_tract(census_pop * hotspot),
    vulnerable_exposed=per_tract(vulnerable_pop * hotspot),
    deprived_pct=np.where(tracts.households > 0, 100 * tracts.deprived_share, np.nan),
)
city_tracts = gpd.clip(city_tracts[city_tracts.residents >= 1], city.union_all(),
                       keep_geom_type=True)
by_exposed = city_tracts.exposed.sort_values(ascending=False).cumsum()
tracts_half_exposed = int((by_exposed < by_exposed.iloc[-1] / 2).sum()) + 1
by_vulnerable = city_tracts.vulnerable_exposed.sort_values(ascending=False).cumsum()
tracts_half_vulnerable = int((by_vulnerable < by_vulnerable.iloc[-1] / 2).sum()) + 1

# Hotspot outlines inside the city, traced along pixel edges.
city_transform = rasterio.windows.transform(city_win, GRID_TRANSFORM)
hot_in_city = (hotspot & in_city)[city_rows, city_cols].astype("uint8")
hotspot_outline = gpd.GeoSeries(
    [shapely.geometry.shape(g) for g, _ in
     shapes(hot_in_city, mask=hot_in_city == 1, transform=city_transform)],
    crs="EPSG:4326",
).boundary


def rounded_up(x):
    """x rounded up to two significant figures."""
    step = 10 ** (math.floor(math.log10(x)) - 1)
    return math.ceil(x / step) * step


def quantile_norm(values, steps=MAP_STEPS, top=1.0):
    """Color steps that hold about equal numbers of values, at rounded edges.

    The last step ends at the `top` quantile; values above it share the
    colorbar's extension.
    """
    v = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    v = v[np.isfinite(v)]
    inner = np.quantile(v, np.linspace(0, 1, steps + 1)[1:-1])
    upper = rounded_up(np.quantile(v, top))
    edges = np.unique([0.0, *(float(f"{e:.2g}") for e in inner), upper])
    return BoundaryNorm(edges, 256, extend="max" if v.max() > upper else "neither")


def count_ticks(bar):
    """Label a colorbar's steps as whole numbers with thousands separators."""
    bar.ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda x, _: f"{x:,.0f}")


hotspot_halo = [patheffects.withStroke(linewidth=1.8, foreground="white")]
```

Half of the city's residents in hotspots live in `{python} tracts_half_exposed` of the `{python} len(city_tracts)` census radios that reach its urban and peri-urban land.
The median radio has `{python} n(city_tracts.population.median())` census residents, and half of the radios have between `{python} n(city_tracts.population.quantile(0.25))` and `{python} n(city_tracts.population.quantile(0.75))`.
Radios of similar size make a count per radio comparable across the map.

                 cmap=population_cmap, norm=density_norm, zorder=1)

## Vulnerability: who is most at risk?

Exposure asks who is there.
Vulnerability asks who lacks the means to cope.
Coping capacity depends on local incomes, housing, health care, and social ties, which makes any global vulnerability indicator a rough proxy.

This tutorial uses the census index of material deprivation in households, the *Índice de Privación Material de los Hogares* (IPMH).
INDEC publishes it for every tract in the country, and municipal planners already use it.
IPMH places each household in one of four categories:

1. Without deprivation.
2. Deprivation of current resources only, which tracks household income and employment.
3. Deprivation of property resources only, which tracks the quality of the dwelling and its services.
4. Convergent deprivation, both at once.

The analysis counts the residents of households in categories 2, 3, and 4 as vulnerable.
It applies each tract's share of households in those categories to the people the dasymetric step places in that tract.
That share describes households, not people, and larger households weigh more in it than the step assumes.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Other vulnerability measures

Where a census index does not exist, consider one of these:

- The [Relative Wealth Index](https://dataforgood.facebook.com/dfg/tools/relative-wealth-index) from Meta, a global estimate on a grid of about 2.4 km.
- Informal settlement boundaries, such as Argentina's [RENABAP](https://www.argentina.gob.ar/habitat/renabap) registry.
- Age structure from a census, since people over 65 and young children face higher physiological risk.
- Housing quality from local surveys or building permits.

Each one is a proxy, and none captures the full picture.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Local knowledge comes first

A deprivation index finds patterns, but it misses what decides a heat emergency.
It cannot tell you which air conditioners work or which older residents live alone.
Nor does it show which streets have active neighbor networks, or which workers cannot leave their posts in the heat.
Municipal staff, community health workers, and neighborhood organizations know these things.
Use this analysis to direct their attention, not to replace their knowledge.
:::

```{python}
#| label: tbl-vulnerability
#| tbl-cap: "Census population, vulnerable population, and the share of each in hotspots, per urban class. The inequity ratio divides the vulnerable share in hotspots by the overall share. Above 1, vulnerable residents live in hotspots more often than their neighbors."
total_pop, hot_pop = by_class(census_pop)
total_vul, hot_vul = by_class(vulnerable_pop)
vulnerability = pd.DataFrame({
    "class": URBAN_CLASSES,
    "population": total_pop, "exposed": hot_pop,
    "vulnerable": total_vul, "vulnerable_exposed": hot_vul,
}).assign(
    exposed_share=lambda d: 100 * d.exposed / d.population,
    vulnerable_exposed_share=lambda d: 100 * d.vulnerable_exposed / d.vulnerable,
    inequity=lambda d: d.vulnerable_exposed_share / d.exposed_share,
)
deprivation_rate = 100 * total_vul.sum() / total_pop.sum()
inequity = vulnerability.set_index("class").inequity
table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Urban class": [plot.URBAN_CLASS_LABELS[c] for c in URBAN_CLASSES],
    "Population": vulnerability.population.round().astype(int),
    "In hotspots (%)": vulnerability.exposed_share,
    "Vulnerable residents": vulnerability.vulnerable.round().astype(int),
    "Vulnerable in hotspots (%)": vulnerability.vulnerable_exposed_share,
    "Inequity ratio": vulnerability.inequity,
})
md_table(table, floatfmt="{:.2f}")
```

About `{python} f"{deprivation_rate:.0f}"`% of urban residents live in a household with some material deprivation.
In the city's urban class, the inequity ratio reaches `{python} f"{inequity['urbana']:.2f}"`, and in the peri-urban class `{python} f"{inequity['periurbana']:.2f}"`.
At those values, a vulnerable resident is more likely than a neighbor to live in a hotspot.
In the rural settlements the ratio is `{python} f"{inequity['urbano en ruralidad']:.2f}"`.
Use these ratios to rank places for a closer look, not as a count of people at risk.

Right, vulnerable residents who live in hotspots, summed per census radio. Sources: INDEC census 2022; GHS-POP R2023A; Landsat LST P95 composite; Municipalidad de Pergamino; imagery from Esri."
#| fig-alt: "Two maps of the city of Pergamino over grey imagery, shaded by census radio in violets. The left map shows the share of households with material deprivation, lowest in the center and highest in radios on the fringe, with thin magenta hotspot outlines that fall mostly on those darker fringe radios. The right map shows vulnerable residents in hotspots, near zero across the core and darkest in radios along the western, northern and southern edges."
VULNERABLE_COLOR = "#6250d6"
vulnerability_cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list(
    "vulnerability", ["#ecebfa", VULNERABLE_COLOR, "#22186a"]
)
share_norm = quantile_norm(city_tracts.deprived_pct)
vulnerable_norm = quantile_norm(city_tracts.vulnerable_exposed)

fig, (ax_s, ax_e) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.9))
for ax, column, norm, label in [
    (ax_s, "deprived_pct", share_norm, "Households with material deprivation (%)"),
    (ax_e, "vulnerable_exposed", vulnerable_norm,
     "Vulnerable residents in hotspots, per census radio"),
]:
    plot.frame(ax, city_frame, margin=0.01)
    plot.basemap(ax, dim=0.6, credit=ax is ax_e)
    city_tracts.plot(ax=ax, column=column, cmap=vulnerability_cmap, norm=norm,
                     edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.4, zorder=1)
    city_outline.plot(ax=ax, color=plot.INK, linewidth=0.5, zorder=4)
    plot.scalebar(ax)
    bar = plot.colorbar_below(ax, plt.cm.ScalarMappable(norm, vulnerability_cmap), label,
                              ticks=norm.boundaries, extend=norm.extend)
    count_ticks(bar)
hotspot_outline.plot(ax=ax_s, color=plot.HOTSPOT_COLOR, linewidth=0.7, zorder=3,
                     path_effects=hotspot_halo)
ax_s.set_title("Material deprivation vs. hotspots")
ax_e.set_title("Vulnerable residents in hotspots, per census radio")
plot.north_arrow(ax_e)
fig.legend(handles=[plot.legend_line(plot.HOTSPOT_COLOR, "Hotspot outline", 1.2)],
           loc="outside lower center", fontsize=8)
plot.suptitle(fig, "Vulnerability and hotspots meet in a few radios on the city's edge")
plt.show()
```

Half of the vulnerable residents in the city's hotspots live in `{python} tracts_half_vulnerable` of its `{python} len(city_tracts)` radios.

## Risk by barrio

The barrio is the unit that municipal staff and residents recognize.
The code rasterizes the `{python} len(barrios)` barrios onto the LST grid and sums each layer inside them.
A barrio with fewer than `{python} MIN_BARRIO_POPULATION` residents drops out of the ranking.

```{python}
#| label: barrios
barrio_id = burn(((g, i + 1) for i, g in enumerate(barrios.geometry)), dtype="int32")
nb = len(barrios) + 1


def per_barrio(values, where=None):
    """Sum values per barrio, optionally only where a mask holds."""
    v = np.nan_to_num(values) if where is None else np.nan_to_num(values) * where
    return np.bincount(barrio_id.ravel(), weights=v.ravel(), minlength=nb)[1:]


pixels = per_barrio(np.ones(GRID_SHAPE))
barrio_risk = barrios[["nombre"]].assign(
    population=per_barrio(census_pop),
    exposed=per_barrio(census_pop, hotspot),
    vulnerable_exposed=per_barrio(vulnerable_pop, hotspot),
    mean_lst=per_barrio(lst) / per_barrio(np.isfinite(lst)),
    canopy=100 * per_barrio(canopy_share) / per_barrio(np.isfinite(canopy_share)),
    hotspot_share=100 * per_barrio(hotspot) / pixels,
)
barrio_risk["exposed_share"] = 100 * barrio_risk.exposed / barrio_risk.population
barrio_risk = (
    barrio_risk[barrio_risk.population >= MIN_BARRIO_POPULATION]
    .sort_values("exposed", ascending=False)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
top3 = barrio_risk.head(3)
top5_share = 100 * barrio_risk.exposed.head(5).sum() / barrio_risk.exposed.sum()
numbered_share = (
    100 * barrio_risk.exposed.head(NUMBERED_BARRIOS).sum() / barrio_risk.exposed.sum()
)
```

    edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.8, zorder=1,

ranked[ranked.exposed.isna()].plot(
    ax=ax, facecolor="white", edgecolor=plot.MUTED, hatch="////", linewidth=0.5,
    alpha=0.8, zorder=1,

for row in ranked[ranked["rank"] <= NUMBERED_BARRIOS].itertuples():
    point = row.geometry.representative_point()
    ax.annotate(f"{row.rank:.0f}", (point.x, point.y), ha="center", va="center",
                fontsize=8, fontweight="semibold", color=plot.INK, zorder=5,
                bbox={"boxstyle": "circle,pad=0.25", "fc": "white", "ec": plot.INK, "lw": 0.6})

Together, the top five barrios hold `{python} f"{top5_share:.0f}"`% of all the city's residents in hotspots.
Size matters as much as heat in this ranking.
A large barrio with a modest hot share can place above a small one that is mostly hot.
Read the share column in the table beside the count before you choose where to start.

## Recommendations

This section turns the findings into actions that hold under every emissions scenario.
Each recommendation points to the finding behind it.
For the policy reasoning behind decisions under deep uncertainty, see the companion material in the [Great Data Products episode](https://greatdataproducts.com/episodes/2026/09/wesley-heat-data/).

### 1. Adopt a heat emergency plan

Set clear thresholds that activate an emergency response, and coordinate them across municipal departments.

- Use the baseline of `{python} f"{baseline_days:.0f}"` days a year above 35 °C to separate a normal summer from an emergency.
- Stage water, shade, and cooling points in the barrios at the top of @tbl-barrios before the season starts.
- Send early warnings through several channels, and target the barrios with high inequity ratios first.

An emergency plan needs little capital and adapts as conditions change, which makes it the right first step under any scenario.

### 2. Reduce risk where exposure and vulnerability meet

Direct capital spending to the barrios that rank high on both residents and vulnerable residents in hotspots.

- Start with `{python} top3.nombre.iloc[0]`, `{python} top3.nombre.iloc[1]`, and `{python} top3.nombre.iloc[2]`.
- Fund green and blue infrastructure there first, and build passive cooling into every new public building.
- Where trees cannot grow, use shade structures and cool materials instead.

Shade, stormwater control, and cleaner air bring benefits even without further warming.
Spending in the highest-risk barrios first puts each peso where heat and people meet.

### 3. Grow a connected tree canopy

Plant and protect trees along corridors that link the hottest barrios to cool public spaces.

- Choose native species that tolerate the hotter climate the projections describe.
- Prioritize the open, bare ground at the fringe, where @fig-drivers shows the highest temperatures.
- Learn from [Medellín's green corridors](https://www.unep.org/en/news-and-stories/story/medellin-shows-how-nature-based-solutions-can-keep-people-and-planet-cool), which the city reports cut its heat island by about 2 °C.

Canopy cools under every scenario.
Under SSP1-2.6 it improves daily life, and under SSP5-8.5 it becomes critical infrastructure.

### 4. Use built and non-structural measures where trees cannot go

Large sheds and industrial yards cannot host a canopy, and @fig-drivers shows that fully roofed pixels heat back up.

- Require reflective roofs on new industrial and commercial buildings.
- Add shade structures over yards and parking where people work outdoors.
- Require cross-ventilation in new housing codes.
- Shift outdoor work schedules on emergency days.

Each measure works on its own and can grow incrementally as budgets allow.

### 5. Educate and engage residents

Build public understanding of heat risk and of what protects people from it.

- Run an awareness campaign before each summer.
- Train community health workers in the priority barrios.
- Hold a yearly workshop for municipal staff on the updated risk maps.
- Publish this analysis, and its code, for anyone to check and repeat.

Understanding builds the political support that sustained investment needs, and it counters the human habit of underpreparing for rare disasters.

### Limits of this analysis

- **Surface is not air.** LST ranks surfaces by heat, and it does not measure the heat stress a person feels.
- **Material deprivation is one part of vulnerability.** IPMH misses age, health, isolation, and outdoor work.
- **Models disagree.** The run-to-run spread in @tbl-projections is wide, especially late in the century.
- **No local knowledge.** Field visits and conversations with residents should test every ranking here.

## Explore the layers

The map below shows the layers from this tutorial over the city.
Use the checkboxes to switch layers on and off, and select a barrio to see its numbers in the side panel.
The map runs in your browser and needs no Python kernel.

```{python}
#| label: map
import base64

import ipywidgets as widgets
from lonboard import BitmapLayer, Map, PolygonLayer
from lonboard.basemap import CartoStyle, MaplibreBasemap
from lonboard.controls import FullscreenControl, NavigationControl, ScaleControl
from PIL import Image


def png_data_uri(rgba):
    buffer = io.BytesIO()
    Image.fromarray(rgba, mode="RGBA").save(buffer, format="PNG", optimize=True)
    return "data:image/png;base64," + base64.b64encode(buffer.getvalue()).decode()


def colorize(values, cmap, norm):
    """Colour an array with a matplotlib colormap; NaN becomes transparent."""
    rgba = plt.get_cmap(cmap)(norm(values), bytes=True)
    rgba[~np.isfinite(values)] = 0
    return rgba


map_bounds =list(rasterio.windows.bounds(city_win, GRID_TRANSFORM))
lst_layer = BitmapLayer(
    image=png_data_uri(colorize(lst[city_rows, city_cols], plot.CMAP_LST, lst_norm)),
    bounds=map_bounds, opacity=0.85, pickable=False,
)
canopy_layer = BitmapLayer(
    image=png_data_uri(colorize(100 * canopy_share[city_rows, city_cols],
                                truncated(plot.CMAP_CANOPY), cover_norm)),
    bounds=map_bounds, opacity=0.9, pickable=False, visible=False,
)

# Buildings travel as a footprint bitmap at 1/8 of an LST pixel. As vectors,
# the city's footprints would add several megabytes to this page.
footprint = rasterize(
    buildings.geometry[buildings.intersects(box(*map_bounds))],
    out_shape=(city_win.height * SUPERSAMPLE, city_win.width * SUPERSAMPLE),
    transform=city_transform * Affine.scale(1 / SUPERSAMPLE), fill=0, dtype="uint8",
)
footprint_rgba = np.zeros((*footprint.shape, 4), dtype="uint8")
footprint_rgba[footprint == 1] = (98, 80, 214, 210)
building_layer = BitmapLayer(
    image=png_data_uri(footprint_rgba), bounds=map_bounds, pickable=False, visible=False
)

hot_city = hotspot[city_rows, city_cols].astype("uint8")
hotspot_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    geometry=[shapely.geometry.shape(g) for g, _ in
              shapes(hot_city, mask=hot_city == 1, transform=city_transform)],
    crs="EPSG:4326",
)
hotspot_layer = PolygonLayer.from_geopandas(
    hotspot_gdf, get_fill_color=[0, 229, 255, 40], get_line_color=[0, 229, 255, 255],
    line_width_min_pixels=1.5, pickable=False,
)

barrio_props = barrio_risk.rename(columns={
    "population": "residents", "exposed": "residents_in_hotspots",
    "vulnerable_exposed": "vulnerable_in_hotspots", "mean_lst": "mean_p95_lst_c",
    "canopy": "canopy_pct",
})
barrio_gdf = barrios[["nombre", "geometry"]].merge(
    barrio_props[["nombre", "residents", "residents_in_hotspots", "vulnerable_in_hotspots",
                  "mean_p95_lst_c", "canopy_pct"]].round(1),
    on="nombre", how="left",
)
barrio_layer = PolygonLayer.from_geopandas(
    barrio_gdf, filled=True, get_fill_color=[0, 0, 0, 0], get_line_color=[20, 20, 20, 230],
    line_width_min_pixels=1.2, auto_highlight=True, highlight_color=[255, 255, 255, 70],
)

layers = {
    "Surface temperature (P95)": lst_layer,
    "Canopy cover": canopy_layer,
    "Buildings (Overture)": building_layer,
    "Hotspots (cyan outline)": hotspot_layer,
    "Barrios": barrio_layer,
}
cx, cy = (map_bounds[0] + map_bounds[2]) / 2, (map_bounds[1] + map_bounds[3]) / 2
heat_map = Map(
    list(layers.values()),
    basemap=MaplibreBasemap(style=CartoStyle.Positron),
    view_state={"longitude": cx, "latitude": cy, "zoom": 12.3},
    controls=[NavigationControl(), ScaleControl(position="bottom-left"), FullscreenControl()],
    height=600,
)
toggles = []
for name, layer in layers.items():
    toggle = widgets.Checkbox(value=layer.visible, description=name, indent=False,
                              layout=widgets.Layout(width="auto", margin="0 16px 0 0"))
    widgets.jslink((toggle, "value"), (layer, "visible"))
    toggles.append(toggle)


def gradient(cmap, norm, title, unit, start=0.0):
    """A small HTML colour ramp for the map legend."""
    stops = ", ".join(
        f"rgb({r * 255:.0f},{g * 255:.0f},{b * 255:.0f})"
        for r, g, b, _ in plt.get_cmap(cmap)(np.linspace(start, 1, 8))
    )
    lo, hi = norm.boundaries[0], norm.boundaries[-1]
    return (
        f"<div style='display:inline-block;margin-right:24px;font-size:12px'>{title}<br>"
        f"<span style='display:inline-block;width:160px;height:10px;"
        f"background:linear-gradient(90deg,{stops})'></span><br>"
        f"<span>{lo:g}</span><span style='float:right'>{hi:g} {unit}</span></div>"
    )


legend = widgets.HTML(
    gradient(plot.CMAP_LST, lst_norm, "Surface temperature, P95", "°C")
    + gradient(plot.CMAP_CANOPY, cover_norm, "Canopy cover", "%", start=0.12)
)
widgets.VBox([
    widgets.HBox(toggles, layout=widgets.Layout(flex_flow="row wrap")),
    legend,
    heat_map,
])
```
